original_value: Much HCI research seeks to contribute to technological agendas that lead to more just and participative labor relations and practices, yet that research also raises concerns about forms of exploitation associated with them. In this paper, we explore how U.S. independent [indie] game developers' socio-technological practices inject forms of labor, capital, and production into the game development industry. Our findings highlight that indie game development 1) seeks to promote an alternative to business models of game development that depend on free and immaterial labor; 2) builds offline networks at different scales to develop collectives that can sustain their production; and 3) emphasizes how distributed collaboration, co-creation, and the use of free tools and middleware make game production more widely accessible. The research contributes to HCI research that seeks to explicate and mitigate emerging forms of exploitation enabled by new technologies and processes. Our critical review of indie developers' practices and strategies also extends the current conceptualization of labor and technology in CSCW.

result.paraphrase: Much HCI research aims to support technological agendas that foster more equitable and participatory labor relations and practices, but it also surfaces concerns about exploitation tied to those same agendas. In this paper, we examine how the socio-technological practices of U.S. independent [indie] game developers bring particular forms of labor, capital, and production into the game development industry. Our findings show that indie game development 1) aims to offer an alternative to game development business models reliant on free and immaterial labor; 2) creates offline networks at multiple scales to form collectives capable of sustaining production; and 3) stresses that distributed collaboration, co-creation, and the use of free tools and middleware make game production more broadly accessible. This research contributes to HCI work that seeks to identify and reduce emerging forms of exploitation enabled by new technologies and processes. Our critical review of indie developers’ practices and strategies also broadens current CSCW conceptions of labor and technology.
